title: Muslims as minorities
hookLine: Muslims living as minorities, balancing faith and society

cards: Umm Salamah remembers it in her own words, kept in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad.
A small group of Muslims, pressed hard in Mecca, crossed the sea to Abyssinia, a Christian kingdom ruled by a king known by his title, the Negus.
In paraphrase, she says: we came to the land of Abyssinia, found there the best of neighbors, and could practice our religion in safety. Then envoys arrived from Mecca to have them sent back.
The king called the Muslims in and asked them to speak for themselves. A minority, in a strange land, before a king of another faith.

teach.h: JA'FAR RECITES MARYAM; THE KING WEEPS.
teach.b: Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin, speaks for the group, and the king asks to hear something of their scripture. Ja'far recites from the opening of surah Maryam, about Mary and the birth of Jesus.
Umm Salamah says the king wept until his beard was wet, and refused to hand them over. The minority was protected, in a scene of mutual respect. Muslims draw a principle from texts like this.

A verse of the Qur'an, in paraphrase, says Allah does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who have not fought you over religion or driven you from your homes, and that Allah loves those who deal justly.
Today, Muslims live as minorities in Europe and the Americas, in India and China, in Australia and across Africa.

teach.h: PRAYER AT WORK, EID ON A WORKDAY.
teach.b: The questions are practical: where to pray at work, how to keep Friday prayer with a school schedule, finding halal food, Eid on a working day, a Muslim burial plot, being misunderstood in the news.

Some scholars have built a whole field around these questions, called the fiqh of minorities. Others hold that the classical schools already have what is needed. Both are answering the same family's questions.
Day to day, it looks like this. A Muslim nurse prays in a supply room on her break. A family explains Ramadan at a school meeting.
A mosque opens its doors to the neighbors on Eid.
Small, steady negotiations, made with a neighbor who may become, as Umm Salamah put it, the best of neighbors.

how: Muslims living as minorities pray at work or school where space allows, look for halal food and Muslim burial, arrange leave for Friday prayer and Eid, and often open their mosques to neighbors; some follow scholars of the 'fiqh of minorities', others the classical schools directly.

Muslims living where Islam is banned by law
Muslims keeping faith among other-faith neighbors

games.q: you're Ja'far, standing before a Christian king who asks to hear your scripture. what do you recite?
o: the opening of surah Maryam, about Mary and Jesus.
games.why: in Umm Salamah's account he recites from surah Maryam, and the king weeps until his beard is wet.

practice: Picture the small group arriving by sea in Abyssinia, carrying very little, not knowing who will welcome them.

Then let the picture move to today: a family whose hijab is the only one at the grocery store, or the only family skipping lunch through Ramadan. If you pray, ask for good for them and for their neighbors, in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Muslims as minorities. From companions sheltered in Abyssinia to families today in Europe, the Americas, India, China and beyond, keeping faith among neighbors of other faiths. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a minority; the word in fiqh al-aqalliyyat, the fiqh of minorities.

carryVoice: Your line: faith as a minority. Any neighbor can become the best of neighbors. Next, a new stretch: science and faith.
